notes.title: Why delivery is never perfect
notes.html:
Networks lose packets and acknowledgements, and processes crash between "did the work" and "told anyone". So a sender can never be sure whether a message arrived. This is the Two Generals problem: you can't have certainty with an unreliable channel.

Consider the consumer crash windows: (A) crash before doing the work, (B) crash after the work but before the ack/commit. In (B) the broker will redeliver, and the work is done twice.

Worked example. Payment consumer debits 500 rupees, then crashes before committing the offset. On restart it reads the same message and debits again: 1,000 charged. This is real; it is why every payment system obsesses over idempotency.

Industry examples. Stripe, Razorpay, PayU and UPI rails all publish rules for duplicate protection (idempotency keys, transaction reference IDs) because retries are expected.

Everyday analogy. You post a letter and do not hear back. Resend it and risk two copies, or do not and risk none.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming a design "never duplicates".
  • Not identifying where exactly the crash windows are.

notes.title: At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once
notes.html:
Three delivery guarantees:

  • At-most-once: send, never retry. Can lose messages, never duplicates. Commit offset first, then process. Fine for metrics, logs, GPS pings.
  • At-least-once: retry until acknowledged. Never loses, may duplicate. Process first, then commit. The default for most real systems.
  • Exactly-once: each message's effect happens once. Not achievable as pure delivery over an unreliable network; achievable as effect by combining at-least-once with idempotent or transactional processing.
Guarantee Loses data Duplicates Cost
At-most-once Yes No Cheapest
At-least-once No Yes Needs dedup
Exactly-once effect No No (effect) Extra state, latency

Gravity. Default to at-least-once plus idempotent consumers. It is the most robust approach and easy to reason about. Reverting later is easy since the architecture does not change; adding idempotency afterwards means changing every side effect.

Worked example. Likes counter: duplicates inflate by 0.01%: acceptable with at-most/at-least. Bank transfer: not acceptable; needs an effect-once design.

Industry examples. Kafka's default producer/consumer pattern is at-least-once; SQS Standard is at-least-once; MQTT defines QoS 0, 1 and 2 matching these three.

Everyday analogy. Delivery with a tracking signature: a courier who retries until signed may deliver twice.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up commit-before and commit-after processing.
  • Treating "exactly-once" as a free setting.

notes.title: The exactly-once myth and Kafka's version
notes.html:
"Exactly-once delivery" is a marketing phrase. What systems really give is exactly-once processing effects within a controlled boundary.

Kafka offers, within Kafka only:

  • Idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true, default in modern clients): each producer gets a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers; the broker drops duplicates from retries. Removes duplicates and reordering from producer retries.
  • Transactions (transactional.id): atomically write to several partitions and commit consumer offsets together; readers use isolation.level=read_committed. This enables consume-process-produce pipelines (Kafka Streams processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2).

The guarantee ends at Kafka's edge. If your processor also calls a payment API or writes to MySQL, those side effects are outside the transaction and can still be repeated; there you need idempotency keys or a transactional outbox/inbox.

Worked example. Stream job reads orders, writes order_totals. With EOS v2, a crash mid-way aborts the transaction; the output messages written are invisible to read_committed consumers and the input offset is not advanced, so the retry produces the totals once. But if the job also POSTs to an email provider, an email can go twice.

Industry examples. Confluent popularised this in Kafka 0.11 (2017). Flink offers exactly-once via checkpoints plus two-phase commit sinks.

Everyday analogy. Trading cards only counted once if you stamp them in the same room that holds the album; outside that room, stamps are not tracked.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "Kafka gives exactly-once, done" when the sink is an external system.
  • Forgetting read_committed on consumers; otherwise aborted data is visible.

notes.title: Idempotency and dedup keys
notes.html:
An operation is idempotent if doing it twice gives the same result as doing it once. SET balance=500 is idempotent; balance = balance - 100 is not. The practical technique: give every logical operation a unique idempotency key and remember which keys you have already processed.

Design:

  1. Client generates a key (UUID) per intended action and reuses it on retry (Stripe Idempotency-Key header).
  2. Server stores key -> result in a table with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the side effect.
  3. On a repeat key, return the stored result without redoing work.
  4. Expire keys after a window (Stripe keeps them about 24 hours).
CREATE TABLE processed_messages (
  msg_id   TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  result   JSONB,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);

BEGIN;
INSERT INTO processed_messages(msg_id) VALUES ('evt_123');  -- fails on duplicate
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 7;
COMMIT;

Other tricks: natural keys (order ID plus event type), conditional writes (UPDATE ... WHERE version = 3), upserts, and using the Kafka coordinates (topic, partition, offset) as a dedup key.

Worked example. A consumer sees payment-captured for order 42 twice. First: inserts key (42, captured) and updates the order. Second: insert hits the unique constraint; code treats it as "already done" and acks. Table growth: 10M messages/day x 50 bytes = 500 MB/day, so TTL-clean after 7 days (3.5 GB).

Gravity. The dedup record and the side effect must commit atomically, otherwise the crash window returns. In a different store (Redis SETNX then DB write), you again have a window. Prefer same-database dedup.

Industry examples. Stripe idempotency keys; AWS SQS FIFO MessageDeduplicationId (5 min window); Razorpay and UPI use reference IDs; Kafka idempotent producers.

Everyday analogy. A cinema ticket with a number: scanning the same ticket twice at the gate does not let two people in.

Common interview traps.

  • Checking "have I seen this?" with a read, then writing later (race). Use a unique constraint.
  • Generating a new key on each client retry, which defeats the purpose.
  • Dedup window shorter than the maximum redelivery delay.

notes.title: Putting it together: a safe consumer
notes.html:
Recipe for a reliable consumer: at-least-once delivery, idempotent handler, commit after success, retries with backoff, DLQ for poison messages.

void onMessage(ConsumerRecord<String, Event> r) {
  try (var tx = db.begin()) {
    if (!tx.insertIfAbsent("processed", r.value().id())) { ack(r); return; } // duplicate
    applyBusinessLogic(r.value(), tx);
    tx.commit();
  } catch (TransientException e) { throw e; }   // retry later
  catch (PermanentException e) { sendToDlq(r, e); }
  ack(r);
}

Worked example. 1,000 msgs/s, 0.1% duplicates = 1 duplicate/s: dedup insert adds about 1 ms per message. The unique index lookup is cheap relative to the cost of a double charge.

Gravity. This pattern is reversible and cheap to adopt per service; skipping it is the expensive choice when the first incident arrives.

Industry examples. Payment processors, ledger services and order systems (Shopify, Uber) all follow "at-least-once plus idempotent writes".

Everyday analogy. A bank teller who checks the cheque number against the "already cashed" ledger before paying.

Common interview traps.

  • Acking before the DB commit (data loss).
  • Not distinguishing transient from permanent errors.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Crash windows between work and ack make duplicates unavoidable; plan for them.
  • At-most-once may lose, at-least-once may duplicate; exactly-once is an effect achieved by dedup or transactions.
  • Kafka EOS (idempotent producer, transactions, read_committed) works only inside Kafka; external side effects need their own idempotency.
  • Idempotency key plus a unique constraint, committed atomically with the side effect, is the core technique.
  • Default recipe: at-least-once, idempotent handler, commit after, backoff retry, DLQ.

questions.promptHtml: Why can't a message system guarantee that a message is delivered exactly once? Where exactly do duplicates come from?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundational reasoning: can the candidate locate the crash windows rather than recite slogans?

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Networks lose packets and acknowledgements, and processes crash between doing the work and telling anyone. The sender cannot distinguish "the message was lost" from "the ack was lost" (the Two Generals problem). So a reliable system retries, and a retry after a lost ack duplicates the work. The key crash window is after the side effect and before the commit/ack.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Consumer crash windows: (A) crash before doing the work: the broker redelivers, no harm. (B) crash after the work but before the commit: the broker redelivers and the work is done twice. Producer side: the broker stored the message but the ack was lost, so the producer retries and the broker has two copies.

Producer -> Broker -> Consumer -> Database
                          ^ crash here after DB write, before offset commit => redelivery

Example: a consumer debits 500, crashes before committing the offset, restarts and debits again: 1,000 charged.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming a design "never duplicates".
  • Not naming the crash window.
  • Assuming a broker setting can fix an application-side window.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where else do duplicates arise? -> Client retries on timeout, relay re-publishing, rebalance reassigning an uncommitted batch.
  2. Can you make the window zero? -> Not across two systems; you make the effect idempotent.
  3. Why do payment APIs have idempotency keys? -> Retries are expected and double charges are unacceptable.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use acks". Senior: names both crash windows, the Two Generals limit and that the fix is at the effect, not the channel.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Every payment incident postmortem about double debit traces back to a crash window B with a non-idempotent handler.

questions.promptHtml: Define at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once. How do offset commits map to each, and which do you default to?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common, but many candidates mix up commit-before and commit-after.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: At-most-once: commit first, then process; a crash loses messages but never duplicates. At-least-once: process, then commit; a crash causes redelivery, so duplicates are possible but loss is not. Exactly-once is not achievable as pure delivery; I achieve it as an effect by combining at-least-once with idempotent or transactional processing. My default is at-least-once with idempotent consumers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Guarantee Loses data Duplicates Cost
At-most-once Yes No Cheapest
At-least-once No Yes Needs dedup
Exactly-once effect No No (effect) Extra state, latency

Use at-most-once for metrics, GPS pings, logs, where a rare loss is fine. A likes counter with 0.01% inflation is tolerable; a bank transfer is not. Moving between the first two later is a one-line commit order change; adding idempotency to every side effect afterward is expensive, so I design it in early.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Swapping commit-before and commit-after.
  • Treating exactly-once as a free setting.
  • Choosing at-most-once for money.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. MQTT QoS 0/1/2? -> At-most, at-least, and a 4-way handshake exactly-once on the hop only.
  2. SQS Standard vs FIFO? -> Standard at-least-once; FIFO adds ordering and a 5-minute dedup window.
  3. How do you test this? -> Kill the consumer between the effect and the commit in a test and assert the final state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: definitions. Senior: defaults, cost per guarantee, and the effect-versus-delivery distinction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team chose at-most-once for "speed" and lost refund events; reconciliation found them weeks later.

questions.contextHtml: Three consumers on one platform: (1) GPS pings from 1M scooters every 2 s for a live map; (2) a "like" counter; (3) wallet transfers between users. An engineer wants a single global setting: "exactly-once everywhere, it is the safest".
questions.promptHtml: Choose a guarantee for each and push back on the global setting.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Accepts exactly-once everywhere without cost or semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does a lost or duplicate event cost for each? What is the latency budget? Are there external side effects?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Value per message differs by orders of magnitude, so the guarantee should too.
  4. How I'd verify: Estimate the cost of 0.01% duplicates or loss per case; measure latency overhead of transactions in a test.
  5. Root cause (reasoning): GPS: at-most-once; a missed ping is replaced 2 s later, and 500k msg/s is not worth dedup state. Likes: at-least-once with a relaxed count or a set-based dedup, or accept 0.01% error. Transfers: at-least-once plus idempotency key and a unique constraint in the same DB transaction, an exactly-once effect.
  6. Fix (answer): Different guarantees per flow, documented in a table.
  7. Prevention: A design-review checklist asking "what happens on duplicate and on loss?".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a global exactly-once: it adds latency and state, still ends at system boundaries, and wastes cost where loss is harmless.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• GPS feeds billing later? -> Then the semantics change; store raw events at-least-once.
  • Likes shown with exact counts to creators? -> Dedup by (user, post) unique key.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a global "safe" transactional setting cut a telemetry pipeline's throughput by 40% for no benefit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: exactly-once everywhere.
  • Hire: matches each to a guarantee with reasons.
  • Strong hire: quantifies cost, mentions effect-based exactly-once and review checklist.

questions.promptHtml: How do you design an idempotent endpoint or consumer using an idempotency key? What are the pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Idempotency is the practical core of reliable systems; details decide correctness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The client generates a unique key per intended action and reuses it on every retry. The server stores the key with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the side effect. A repeat key returns the stored result without redoing the work. Keys expire after a window longer than the worst redelivery delay.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SET balance = 500 is naturally idempotent, balance = balance - 100 is not. Make the second kind safe with a dedup record:

CREATE TABLE processed_messages (
  msg_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  result JSONB,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now()
);
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO processed_messages(msg_id) VALUES ('evt_123'); -- fails on duplicate
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 7;
COMMIT;

Other tools: natural keys (orderId + eventType), conditional writes (WHERE version = 3), upserts, and Kafka coordinates (topic, partition, offset). Table growth: 10M msgs/day x 50 B = 500 MB/day; keep 7 days = 3.5 GB.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Read-then-write check (race); use the unique constraint.
  • New key on every retry.
  • Dedup window shorter than max redelivery delay.
  • Dedup in a different store from the side effect.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Same key, different payload? -> Reject (422) or compare a payload hash.
  2. Concurrent duplicates in flight? -> The unique insert blocks one; return "in progress" or wait.
  3. How long to keep keys? -> Longer than the max retry horizon (Stripe about 24 h).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "store a UUID". Senior: atomic with the side effect, in-flight handling, payload mismatch, TTL sizing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "seen" check in Redis followed by a DB write caused rare double bookings during Redis failover.

questions.contextHtml:
Consumers are idempotent "by design" yet customers occasionally receive two refunds. Two consumers (partition rebalance during a deploy) process the same refund event concurrently.

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void onRefund(RefundEvent e) {
  if (!db.exists("processed", e.id())) {        // 1. check
    paymentApi.refund(e.orderId(), e.amount()); // 2. side effect
    db.insert("processed", e.id());             // 3. record
  }
}
fun onRefund(e: RefundEvent) {
  if (!db.exists("processed", e.id)) {          // 1. check
    paymentApi.refund(e.orderId, e.amount)      // 2. side effect
    db.insert("processed", e.id)                // 3. record
  }
}
questions.promptHtml: What are the bugs and how do you fix them?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says the check exists so it is fine, or adds a lock in memory.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the payment API support idempotency keys? Single DB or distributed? How many consumers can see the same event (rebalance)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Find duplicated refunds via the payment provider report and reverse them; pause the deploy-induced rebalances.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-act race between two consumers; (b) crash between step 2 and 3 repeats the refund; (c) clock/ordering irrelevant (red herring).
  4. How I'd verify: Query for event ids with two refund ids; look at timestamps and consumer ids in logs.
  5. Root cause: The check and the record are not atomic with the side effect; and step 2 is external, so a local transaction cannot cover it.
  6. Fix: Insert the key first with a unique constraint (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, check rows affected) and pass the event id as the payment API's idempotency key so the provider also dedups. If the insert says "already exists with status DONE" ack; if "IN_PROGRESS" retry later.
  7. Prevention: A test that runs two consumers on the same event; reconciliation job.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A JVM lock or Redis SETNX only; they fail across processes or failovers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Provider has no idempotency key? -> Record intent first (status PENDING), query the provider by reference before retrying.
  • Stuck IN_PROGRESS rows? -> Timeout and reconcile.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a "has this been processed" check passed in both pods within the same 20 ms during a rebalance.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: calls it safe.
  • Hire: unique constraint and key-first approach.
  • Strong hire: pairs it with a provider idempotency key, in-progress state and reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: A Kafka Streams job reads orders, enriches, writes order_totals, and also calls an email vendor and updates a MySQL table. The architect writes in the design doc: "processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2, so every email is sent exactly once". After a broker failover, a few customers got two confirmation emails and a MySQL counter is off by 17.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and what is the right design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames a Kafka bug or suggests turning off retries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which sinks are inside Kafka? Does the vendor accept an idempotency key? Does MySQL write share a transaction with anything?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Apologise via support; stop counter drift by recomputing it from order_totals.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: EOS only covers read-process-write inside Kafka; email and MySQL are outside the transaction.
  4. How I'd verify: Trace the duplicate emails to a task restart; check the read_committed setting on consumers of order_totals.
  5. Root cause: When a transaction aborts and the task re-runs, Kafka output is rolled back, but the email and MySQL writes already happened and happen again.
  6. Fix: Emit an EmailRequested event to a topic (inside EOS) and have a separate idempotent sender use the event id as the vendor's idempotency key / a dedup table; derive MySQL counters via an idempotent upsert keyed by event id, or keep counters in the stream state.
  7. Prevention: Design doc template stating boundaries of each guarantee; isolation.level=read_committed on downstream consumers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not claim exactly-once to stakeholders; not remove the retries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Without read_committed downstream? -> Aborted records are visible: duplicates and phantom data.
  • Cost of EOS? -> Transaction overhead and latency (commit interval).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: "exactly-once" in the slide deck became "twice" in a customer's inbox.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames Kafka.
  • Hire: explains the boundary and adds idempotency.
  • Strong hire: redesigns side effects as events with dedup and notes read_committed.

questions.promptHtml: How do the Kafka idempotent producer and transactions work, and what exactly do they guarantee?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates "Kafka has exactly-once" from knowing the mechanism and its boundary.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With enable.idempotence=true each producer gets a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers, so the broker drops duplicates caused by retries and keeps order. Transactions (transactional.id) let me atomically write to several partitions and commit consumer offsets together; consumers with isolation.level=read_committed see only committed data. Together they give exactly-once for consume-process-produce inside Kafka only; external side effects are not covered.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Idempotence handles one producer session to one partition. A transaction coordinator tracks the transaction, writes commit/abort markers into the partitions, and a transactional.id fences zombie instances (epoch bump). Kafka Streams enables this with processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2. After a crash mid-transaction, written output stays invisible to read_committed readers and the input offset is not advanced, so the retry yields the totals once. Flink achieves exactly-once through checkpoints plus two-phase commit sinks.

Input topic -> Processor -> Output topic
                  |-> offsets committed in the SAME transaction

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting read_committed on consumers.
  • Believing the DB/email/API write joins the transaction.
  • Reusing one transactional.id across live instances (fencing kills one).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is zombie fencing? -> A new producer with the same transactional.id bumps the epoch so the old one's writes are rejected.
  2. Cost? -> Latency from commit markers and a transactional commit interval; throughput hit is modest but real.
  3. How would you extend exactly-once to MySQL? -> Idempotent upsert by event id or store offsets in MySQL in the same transaction.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "enable idempotence". Senior: describes sequence numbers, epochs, markers and the boundary.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A pipeline with EOS but no read_committed consumers exposed aborted records to a downstream dashboard.

questions.contextHtml:
A webhook receiver dedups events in a table with a 5-minute TTL on event_id (copied from an SQS FIFO setup). A partner's system had an outage; when it recovered it replayed events from the last 6 hours. Result: 9,300 orders created twice. Logs:

INSERT processed(event_id=evt_7731) ok   at 09:02
...
INSERT processed(event_id=evt_7731) ok   at 14:41   -- key already expired
questions.promptHtml: Root cause, fix, and how do you clean up?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the TTL" without a principled bound or cleanup plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the partner's max replay horizon? Is there a natural business key (partner order id)? Are duplicates detectable after the fact?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the replay, identify duplicates by (partner, order_ref), cancel/merge the 9,300 duplicates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: TTL shorter than redelivery horizon; event ids regenerated by the partner (would defeat the key); race.
  4. How I'd verify: Compare event ids and payload hashes of the duplicates.
  5. Root cause: Dedup window 5 min vs a 6-hour redelivery delay.
  6. Fix: Dedup on a durable business key with a unique constraint on the orders table itself (UNIQUE(partner_id, partner_order_ref)), and keep event ids for at least the longest realistic replay (7 days, 10M/day x 50 B = 3.5 GB, cheap).
  7. Prevention: Contract with the partner on replay behaviour; alert on duplicate-key hits spike; test with a replay.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not an infinite window of event ids; the unique business key gives permanent protection cheaply.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Partner re-sends with new event ids? -> Only a business key protects you.
  • How to expire? -> Partition tables by day and drop old partitions.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a dedup TTL tuned for a queue was reused for a webhook and broke the first time a partner retried after an outage.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: arbitrary TTL bump.
  • Hire: ties window to replay horizon and uses a business key.
  • Strong hire: also cleanup, sizing math and partner contract.

questions.contextHtml:
Postmortem: 412 customers were debited twice in 90 minutes. Timeline:

11:03 deploy of payment-consumer v52 (rolling)
11:04 consumers rebalance; max.poll.interval.ms=30000; batch processing takes ~45 s
11:05 consumer-3 evicted; its batch reassigned to consumer-5 while consumer-3 still running
11:05 both consumers call the ledger: debit applied twice
11:40 offset commits fail: CommitFailedException

Handler: debit(account, amt), then commitSync().
questions.promptHtml: Write the review: causes, contributing factors, fixes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Human error in the deploy" and "increase the timeout".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did v52 change batch size or per-record time? Is the ledger call idempotent? Did anything gate the rollout on lag or error rate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the rollout, refund via a script with a reconciliation list keyed by message id, communicate to customers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) non-idempotent debit; (b) eviction from slow batches causing double delivery; (c) the deploy itself (trigger, not cause; red herring as root cause).
  4. How I'd verify: Join ledger entries by Kafka offset/message id to find pairs; consumer logs for eviction.
  5. Root cause: At-least-once delivery met a non-idempotent side effect; a zombie consumer kept working after losing its partitions.
  6. Fix: Idempotency key per message in the ledger (unique constraint, same transaction as the debit); smaller max.poll.records; cooperative rebalancing; check partition ownership/fence with a generation id before writing.
  7. Prevention: Chaos test with consumer kills and forced rebalances, reconciliation alerts, rollout gates on duplicate-key metrics.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not just bigger timeouts; they delay detection of real hangs. Not blame; the system allowed it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ledger is a third-party? -> Use the message id as its idempotency key; otherwise an intent table before the call.
  • Would EOS have prevented it? -> No; the ledger is outside Kafka.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: an incident was blamed on a deploy until the timeline showed the real defect had existed for a year.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: human error and timeout bump.
  • Hire: idempotency and eviction mechanism.
  • Strong hire: fencing, chaos tests, reconciliation and honest blameless framing.

questions.contextHtml: A team proposes: "Check Redis SETNX msg:{id} first; if it was set, skip. Then write to Postgres." Throughput is 5,000 msg/s; they say Redis is faster than a DB unique key. Last month a Redis failover happened, and a handful of orders went missing while others duplicated.
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate the design and propose an alternative.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Redis is fast so keep it; add retries."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is Redis persistent/replicated? Is the Postgres write the only side effect? What is the measured cost of the DB insert?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reconcile the failover window by comparing Kafka offsets with Postgres rows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SETNX succeeds then the process crashes before the DB write: the message is skipped forever (loss); (b) failover loses recent keys: duplicates; (c) latency concerns are a red herring.
  4. How I'd verify: Count messages with a Redis key but no row.
  5. Root cause: Dedup state and side effect live in different stores, so no atomicity: two windows (loss and duplicate).
  6. Fix: Put the dedup key in Postgres in the same transaction (INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING); at 5,000 msg/s a unique-index insert is about 1 ms and well within a connection pool; Redis can remain an optional fast-path cache for hot duplicates but never as the source of truth.
  7. Prevention: Reconciliation job and a fault-injection test around failovers.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a distributed lock for dedup; it adds failure modes. If the sink is not a DB, use the sink's conditional write.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 50,000 msg/s? -> Partition dedup tables by key hash, batch inserts, shard Postgres.
  • Sink is Elasticsearch? -> Use the id as the document _id so writes are naturally idempotent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: "fast dedup" in Redis traded a 1 ms cost for a month of reconciliation work.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps Redis.
  • Hire: moves dedup into the same transaction.
  • Strong hire: names both failure windows, quantifies, offers sink-native idempotency.

questions.contextHtml: A processed_messages table (msg_id UUID PK, result JSONB averaging 400 B) holds 90 days of keys at 20M msgs/day. Inserts have slowed from 1 ms to 25 ms, autovacuum is constantly running and the table is 900 GB. Traffic will grow to 200M/day. Max replay horizon is 3 days.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it slow and how do you fix it for 10x?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Add an index or more IOPS.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why 90 days when replay horizon is 3? Is the stored result needed on repeat? Reads vs writes ratio?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Delete old rows in small batches (not one huge DELETE), after confirming the 3-day horizon.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Random UUID PK causes B-tree page splits and cache misses; huge table with dead tuples; the oversized result column.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_user_tables, index size, bloat estimates, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the insert.
  5. Root cause: Retention far beyond need, random keys on a big index, deletes producing bloat. Size now: 20M x 90 x about 450 B = about 810 GB (matches).
  6. Fix: Partition by day and DROP PARTITION after 7 days (keeps 7 x 200M x 450 B = about 630 GB at 10x; drop result or store a small status to cut to about 60 B, about 84 GB); use time-ordered ids (UUIDv7) where possible; keep a unique business key on the main table for permanent protection.
  7. Prevention: Table size alert, retention job monitoring.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not mass DELETE; not removing dedup to "speed up".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need the result on repeat for idempotent API replies? -> Keep a short TTL (24 h) copy only.
  • Postgres is not enough at 200M/day? -> Shard by key hash or use a store with TTL and conditional writes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: dropping a day-partition took milliseconds where the previous batch delete had run all weekend.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds IOPS.
  • Hire: partitions and shortens retention.
  • Strong hire: math, key ordering, thinner rows and permanent business key.

questions.contextHtml:
Code review of a consumer for an order-fulfilment service (1,000 msg/s, 0.1% duplicates expected):

Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
void onMessage(ConsumerRecord<String, Event> r) {
  ack(r);                                      // A
  try (var tx = db.begin()) {
    applyBusinessLogic(r.value(), tx);         // B
    tx.commit();
  } catch (Exception e) {
    log.error("failed", e);                    // C
  }
}
fun onMessage(r: ConsumerRecord<String, Event>) {
  ack(r)                                       // A
  try {
    db.begin().use { tx ->
      applyBusinessLogic(r.value(), tx)        // B
      tx.commit()
    }
  } catch (e: Exception) {
    log.error("failed", e)                     // C
  }
}
questions.promptHtml: List every problem and show the corrected version.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Notices only the log-and-swallow.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What are the transient vs permanent exceptions? Is there a dead-letter topic? Is applyBusinessLogic idempotent by itself?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; review.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Problem 1: ack before commit means any failure loses the message (A). Problem 2: no dedup so redeliveries double-apply. Problem 3: all errors swallowed (C): no retry, no DLQ. Problem 4: no distinction of transient vs permanent errors.
  4. How I'd verify: Fault-injection test that kills the process between ack and commit, and a poison-message test.
  5. Root cause: Wrong order and no error classification.
  6. Fix: In one transaction insert the message id into processed (skip on conflict), apply the logic, commit, then ack; transient exceptions rethrown for retry with backoff, permanent ones go to the DLQ then ack.
  7. Prevention: Shared consumer library enforcing the recipe; tests for crash windows; DLQ alerts.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Dedup lookup costs about 1 ms (1,000 msg/s is trivial); not skipping it because "duplicates are rare": 1 per second is 86,400 per day.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not ack inside the transaction? -> The ack is outside the DB; do it after commit, accepting redelivery handled by dedup.
  • Batch processing? -> Batch the dedup insert and the writes in one transaction and commit offsets after.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a catch-all log.error consumer silently dropped 3% of events for weeks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only spots the swallow.
  • Hire: fixes the order and adds dedup.
  • Strong hire: error classification, DLQ, quantified duplicates and crash-window tests.
